Text: But they just think it's this Black guy in the ditch -- "Hey, oh well."

Speaker: J:
Text: Well, they found out that it was a police officer -- the police officer dies.

Speaker: J:
Text: They charge this guy that they came at with some crime because the police were there because of him.

Speaker: J:
Text: So, my roommate who's in law school and this public defender office that is defending this guy, she takes over the whole case.

Speaker: J:
Text: I mean, she's telling them, she's drawing diagrams, she's telling them who they need to question, and I'm like watching her like "Wow," you know?

Speaker: J:
Text: So that's how I just started just doing it.

Speaker: J:
Text: She just said "Do it" and I did it and it felt good.

Speaker: J:
Text: This guy showed up to my house and I’ve been doing — and I count my years by the festival I actually started a little before then but this was maybe like the seventh, eighth festival — and this guy shows up and he says, "I heard that you help people."

Speaker: J:
Text: And I was like, “Well, yeah, when I can, what do you need?”

Speaker: J:
Text: And he started telling me about his family problems, and I was like, “Well, why are you telling me that?”

Speaker: J:
Text: And he said, “Because they say you help people.”

Speaker: J:
Text: And he meant like, for lack of a better term, like a voodoo person.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, you having a problem.

Speaker: J:
Text: ‘Cause by that time I’d gotten a reputation for helping people, you know, but it was the Union, it was my own labor Union working, Taylor working, that kind of thing.

Speaker: J:
Text: Not like that.

Speaker: J:
Text: But I’ve enjoyed, I really have enjoyed my work.

Speaker: J:
Text: I tell people that God is my supervisor.

Speaker: J:
Text: I have a board of directors but by far they are not my supervisors.

Speaker: J:
Text: I let them think sometime that they kinda running something, but you know God be my supervisor, my supervisor’s given me really good jobs to do, you know with the environment and working with the kids and doing the Fifth Avenue Art Festival and you know, having a chance to work with the elders to do the programs that are done with them.

Speaker: J:
Text: It’s been good.

Speaker: M:
Text: So you grew up Methodist, is that correct?

Speaker: J:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: J:
Text: And I was saying I was born Mary Ann.

Speaker: J:
Text: Okay, so, yes, and I was raised in African Methodist Episcopal — that’s the AME Church — we went to the second and the fourth Sunday and it was a all day affair, I mean all the way from Sunday school to night service and then they had to sanctify people, Holiness people was having Church -- when you passed by their Church, you had to stop by there and finish out the night with that.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, so I was Christian but I started feeling kind of straneg about that probably about 20, 21, you know, and just started -- and I guess it started, well, I read Malcom X and he wasn't Christian, he's gone from being Christian to being a Muslim.

Speaker: J:
Text: So, you know, I started thinking, you know, learning that there were other religions out there.

Speaker: J:
Text: I never did like that "fire and brimstone" and Hell burning stuff, it just always -- I used to have nightmares, you know, from the burning, the Hell burning thing.

Speaker: J:
Text: I mean, I went through like at least a year of dreaming about this big pit that I'd be thrown into and I was just, you know, scared of that.

Speaker: J:
Text: And then when we would go to Holiness churches, they would be shouting and sweating and just jumping all around there.

Speaker: J:
Text: I remember sitting there saying, "Please, please, please, Jesus, please, please don't let it come down on me; please, please, please God, don't let it get on me."

Speaker: J:
Text: "Whatever it is they got, please don't let it get on me."

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, but then when I was 20, mid-twenties, I started looking for God in different churches here in Gainesville.

Speaker: J:
Text: I went to Baptist, to Methodist, to Black, to White -- I mean, I was even at the church that they was calling a cult that's over by the law school.

Speaker: J:
Text: There's a big church over there and they did a story on it because it was cultish here for a while, but I was going to church there, you know.

Speaker: J:
Text: But I never did give up partying totally, you know, and after looking for God all over everywhere, you know, and after they told me it was over there at that church and then I had a birthday party and the people came to get us to go to church and that was on Sunday morning after the Saturday night party and they had spent so much time, you know, on us.

Speaker: J:
Text: We were going to church two or three times a week, you know -- they'd invested time in us and then they'd come and we'd party.

Speaker: J:
Text: They stopped coming and then I started with my name, you know, it was M-A-R-Y-A-N-N, and I was like, "That need to be changed, that look just so common."

Speaker: J:
Text: So then I changed it to M-A-R-I A-N-N, two words, that looked a little better but it just still wasn’t right.

Speaker: J:
Text: So after reading Malcolm and starting getting into African history, I said, “I need my African name.”

Speaker: J:
Text: So I started trying out different names and I came to Qwanda, with a Q, and then I read this book, Jomo Kenyatta, who was the leader of Kenya, and he was a strong leader and I liked his name — no, I’m sorry, not Jomo Kenyatta, it was Nkuma.

Speaker: M:
Text: Oh yeah, okay, yes.

Speaker: J:
Text: It was Nkuma, so I liked that N and K on that, so I put that with Qwanda, NKwanda, and then any name needs to have meaning, so I was looking for God and putting that together and it came out to what I wanted.

Speaker: J:
Text: The meaning I gave to myself, it was for myself, it wasn’t for anybody else, but to remind me of my mission, and my mission is rebirth of the spirit of God, which is love.

Speaker: J:
Text: If I love everything that God made, then I will be doing what God wants me to do.

Speaker: J:
Text: And if I loved everything that God made, then I wouldn’t hurt what God made -- I wouldn’t hurt the air, I wouldn’t hurt the water, I wouldn’t hurt the animals, I wouldn’t hurt other people, so, and Jah is God.

Speaker: J:
Text: And then the NKwanda to me represents a transition —  the NK is from Africa, its Wanda is American, and the Jah is the Caribbean, and it represents that transatlantic trip from Africa to the Caribbean to the United States.

Speaker: J:
Text: So that’s where my name comes from.

Speaker: J:
Text: And I was — I’m a board member of Three Rivers Legal Services and they’re like, you know, provide legal help for the poor, and I was on that board being a poor person, and they wrote me a check because I've been going in the name of NKwanda Jah for two or three years and they wrote me a check to go on a trip and I couldn't cash the check because it said NKwanda Jah and that wasn't my legal name.

Speaker: J:
Text: And they was like, "You need to change your name."

Speaker: J:
Text: Quid pro quo, which was because the director was an attorney -- "I'll go to court with you, you can do that, you know."

Speaker: J:
Text: So, I went to court and the judge said, "Is there -- why are you changing your name?"

Speaker: J:
Text: And I said, "Because I don't wanna die with the slavemaster's name."

Speaker: J:
Text: And he looked at me and looked at the person sitting and says, "Okay."

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, so, so it changed and it's still for me, it's to remind me of all the people always say, "Oh, that is such a pretty name."

Speaker: J:
Text: "I like that."

Speaker: J:
Text: And it's, "Thank you, I appreciate it" but it's really to guide me, you know, to remind me what my purpose is and I do believe that I -- I have to believe, you know, going all the way back to being a high school dropout teen mom, you know, like I said -- I loved school, my parents didn't have to get on me about getting a B, I got on myself.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, so I couldn't understand why something like that would happen to me, and I believe that it had to happen to me because it prepared me for the work that I do now.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, I didn't learn about being a high school dropout from a book or what somebody, you know, told me, you know -- I know about being a teen mom 'cause it ain't nothing I read out of a book, I know, I know what can happen with that.

Speaker: J:
Text: When I taught -- I have another program, my Girl Power program -- what I tell 'em, I tell 'em that I know, not because what somebody told me, you know, so.

Speaker: J:
Text: I've enjoyed it.

Speaker: J:
Text: Being blind, I almost went to school in St. Augustine for the school for the deaf and blind -- that's a really good school there.

Speaker: J:
Text: Ray Charles went to school there.

Speaker: J:
Text: And they wanted me to come to school there when I was in elementary school because of my visual problems but my mom, you know, in our communities you just don't send your child away, I don’t care what’s wrong with ‘em, you don’t send ‘em away.

Speaker: J:
Text: Sometimes, I wonder what my life would have been like, you know, if I had gone to school there as opposed to coming the path that I came.

Speaker: J:
Text: And it’s alright, I like this.

Speaker: J:
Text: I worked, my first twelve years was total volunteerism for this job.

Speaker: J:
Text: Total.

Speaker: J:
Text: And then for five years I got six hundred dollars a year, so it was not until after my twentieth year that I even got a salary for this job.

Speaker: J:
Text: And I used to get up and get dressed — I wouldn’t dress like this in my earlier days, this is a after work or weekend outfit.

Speaker: J:
Text: I got dressed up like everybody else, like I was getting paid.

Speaker: J:
Text: I was at every meeting.

Speaker: J:
Text: And because I’m blind, I don’t drive.

Speaker: J:
Text: I used to be at like ten meetings a day, people would be like, “How’d you get here?”

Speaker: J:
Text: I used to be in ten different cars a day.

Speaker: J:
Text: To get where I needed to get, to do what I needed to do.

Speaker: J:
Text: I loved it, I still love it.

Speaker: J:
Text: Think I’m getting poorer, you know with budget cuts I don’t know how long I’ll be around, but —

Speaker: M:
Text: Oh yeah, those are getting harsh.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, I’ve been blessed that people know me in Gainesville, and they know I work, and they know the work that I’ve done.

Speaker: J:
Text: The majority of City Commissioners who say I can count numbers, as long as I keep my majority of them who know what I’m doing, you know, I’m gonna be somewhat.

Speaker: J:
Text: If something happens I know it’s because they couldn’t — they had to do it, there was no choice.

Speaker: J:
Text: A couple years ago they had me on the third or fourth tier, so they had to go through all these other ones before they even got to where I was, and they didn’t even get close to that.

Speaker: J:
Text: County Commissioner, I can’t say.

Speaker: J:
Text: But the city know where I’m at, know what I’m doing.

Speaker: J:
Text: And I hear my other meeting's coming in, so I mean is there something else?

Speaker: M:
Text: Only if you have any final thoughts to share.

Speaker: J:
Text: I think I’ve — I love Gainesville.

Speaker: J:
Text: I love the diverse culture here.

Speaker: J:
Text: I work with a national organization called Rural Development Leadership Network and we have such a diverse cultural experience, but people in there, you know we have at least ten Native American groups represented in our DLEN.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, Shirley Sharad who was recently in the media is a board member of — Twila, who was one of the few women Indian chiefs, is a board member, so it’s really diverse and I’ve enjoyed that.

Speaker: J:
Text: I mean, Gainesville, I think, prepared me for that because it’s a melting pot here, and I’ve had the pleasure of meeting and working with some really, really great people over my thirty-two years.

Speaker: J:
Text: It’s made the thirty-two years go by fast, you know, I've gotten a lot of support here.

Speaker: J:
Text: I love it.

Speaker: J:
Text: And after all that time — oh I was going to tell you about the God thing, I look for God everywhere, all over Gainesville, and mess around and found God within myself.

Speaker: J:
Text: And I love her dearly.

Speaker: J:
Text: Only time that I went in a church for over twenty years after I found God, it was twenty years before I actually went back and participated.

Speaker: J:
Text: Recently, well not recently, three years ago, joined the church in Atlanta, and it’s called First Afrikan Church and Africa is spelled with a k, there’s a cross there but they’re more ox than crosses.

Speaker: J:
Text: My pastor — and those are words I never, I didn’t think I’d hear myself say for the rest of my life — my pastor, you know teaches more from history books.

Speaker: J:
Text: I mean, you might read the Bible every now and then but that’s just one book and then you got to know where that came from and history of that and, you know, really understand.

Speaker: J:
Text: I didn't even know the King James version was only done in the 1700s.

Speaker: J:
Text: I thought King James version came all the way back from 3 A.D. or something, I didn't even know.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, it's so many things that you don't know, you know, and you don't look at in terms of time and reality, you know.

Speaker: J:
Text: We're fed these fairy tales and this church does not do that in the very least, you know.

Speaker: J:
Text: My pastor, it's nothing for him to miss and use -- and I say miss because he's not trying to do it -- but he might use some profanity, you know, during, because he's explaining stuff, he get caught up, and he curse.

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, I mean, it's nothing for him to try to do some Stevie Wonder or some Marvin Gaye from his pulpit, you know.

Speaker: J:
Text: Or to move the pulpit so the young people can get up and do hip-hop on whatever they're doing in the church, you know.

Speaker: J:
Text: I mean, those are kinds of things -- I don't know if you know about Kwanzaa, but it's a seven-day celebration and for most of African Americans do it that last week of December, from December Christmas Day through January 1st.

Speaker: J:
Text: And this church would do Kwanzaa all year round, and the principles of Kwanzaa, which are Unity, Self-determination, Faith -- I mean, it's seven of them that we do.

Speaker: J:
Text: Or Ujamaa, supporting Black businesses or supporting businesses in your community.

Speaker: J:
Text: If we've done that, we may forever have businesses left down here, you know, so practicing those principles and that's what I've been doing, you know.

Speaker: J:
Text: I think that we're all children of God, that there have been prophets like Jesus, Malcolm, Martin, Sojourner, Ghandi, and others that have given their lives -- they knew that somebody would kill 'em.

Speaker: J:
Text: They knew it, but they kept on going and you know, if -- and I tell people all the time -- I love Jesus more than most Christians do.

Speaker: J:
Text: I respect the work that he did, I want to do and I try to do the work that Jesus did and if all Christians just do the work that he did and not just try to get accolades and jump up and down, and you know like they do for Martin, give all these plaques and everything now, how about Martin, the work that Martin Luther King did?

Speaker: J:
Text: You know, he got killed standing up for some garbage workers.

Speaker: J:
Text: How about let’s do some of that?

Speaker: J:
Text: How about Jesus went out and worked with and tried to help the people who had the plagues, how about how we dealing with people with AIDS, in fact telling ‘em that they’ve done something that God has put a spell on ‘em or something?

Speaker: J:
Text: That’s not my God.

Speaker: J:
Text: My God says that however you know God, however you know God, ‘cause if you know God then you gonna treat what God made right.

Speaker: J:
Text: However you get to know that, if walking around with a stick in your hand all day long gone make you treat people right, walk with the stick.

Speaker: J:
Text: Your walking with the Bible in your hand all day long gonna make you treat people right, walk with the Bible.

Speaker: J:
Text: I don’t care what you’re walking with, long as you come to know and love what God made.

Speaker: J:
Text: Not what man made, not the cars and the trucks and the houses and the clothes.

Speaker: J:
Text: And it only makes sense, right?

Speaker: J:
Text: If you love — like the trees, we can’t live without the trees.

Speaker: J:
Text: We cannot live without trees.

Speaker: J:
Text: You don’t wanna cut ‘em down.

Speaker: J:
Text: For what?

Speaker: J:
Text: To make money?

Speaker: J:
Text: Okay, I’m sorry, I've gone too far now.

Speaker: J:
Text: Oh, I’m preaching now, I gotta go to my meeting but —

Speaker: M:
Text: All right, well thank you very much, this is — I mean it’s been a pleasure, I hope you enjoyed it as well.

Speaker: J:
Text: I have enjoyed it.
